sentences.text: Panoplosaurus was a quadrupedal dinosaur that measured between 5 and 7 meters in length, stood 2 meters tall, and weighed approximately 1.5 to 1.6 tonnes.
Its skull was broad and depressed, narrowing to a blunt, triangular snout.
Bony plates covered the cheeks of this animal.
The scapula and coracoid bones were completely fused, leaving only a slight thickening to mark the suture.
Large, paired osteoderms with a low keel formed bands around the neck extending from the head.
The nasal passage performed two full 360-degree loops in different planes before reaching the olfactory recess.
At 1600 kilograms, the animal was heavier than or equal to its contemporary predators.
Lawrence Lambe discovered the remains in 1917 and formally named the genus Panoplosaurus in 1919.
Charles M. Sternberg found the first fossil in 1917 at Quarry 8 near Little Sandhill Creek.
Sternberg later located a nearly complete skull and skeleton in Quarry 69 of the Belly River Group, 210 feet above sea level.

The holotype specimen CMN 2759 includes a nearly complete skull, most cervical and front dorsal vertebrae with armor, a majority of the forelimb with three articulated fingers, pelvic fragments, foot bones, and hundreds of osteoderms.
Sternberg identified the ilium support structure in 1921, proposing six vertebrae including four true sacrals.
The variability in Panoplosaurus teeth implies a less restrictive feeding strategy than a simple soft-food diet.
Microwear on the teeth indicates a diet of abundant foliage with occasional fruit.
It is uncertain whether Panoplosaurus possessed gastroliths, as they were not identified in the original specimen material.
Panoplosaurus belonged to the family Nodosauridae within the suborder Ankylosauria of the Thyreophora.
Sternberg classified Panoplosaurus within the family Ankylosauridae in 1921.
Sternberg described the genus Edmontonia in 1928 as a close relative of Panoplosaurus.
A 1996 analysis by Yuong-Nam Lee nested Panoplosaurus mirus next to Edmontonia.
A 2003 analysis by Robert Hill and colleagues identified Panoplosaurus as the sister taxon to a group containing Edmontonia and Animantarx.
Modern phylogenetic analyses place Panoplosaurus in the clade Panoplosaurini, close to Edmontonia and Animantarx, but distinct from Nodosaurus and Struthiosaurus.
Panoplosaurus lived in Alberta, Canada, during the Late Cretaceous period.
All known specimens come from the middle Campanian age of the Dinosaur Park Formation, dating to roughly 76 to 75 million years ago.
River channels in the habitat could exceed 200 meters in width and flowed east toward the Bearpaw Sea.
The ground was covered with mosses, lichens, fungi, and decaying plant matter.
The landscape resembled the swampy coastal plains of modern-day Carolina.
The animal lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 79 to 73 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
The genus existed from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
Panoplosaurus mirus is the only known species in the extinct genus Panoplosaurus.
It is debated whether Panoplosaurus and Edmontonia are the same taxon, which has complicated interpretations of their distribution and phylogeny.
Researchers disagree on whether certain specimens, such as ROM 1215, belong to Panoplosaurus or Edmontonia, with some studies retaining them in Panoplosaurus and others moving them to Edmontonia.
It is debated whether the unique short snout of the Panoplosaurus holotype is due to age or sex differences rather than species-specific traits.
Carpenter questioned Sternberg's 1990 identification of four sacrals in Panoplosaurus, noting Edmontonia has only three, though he could not confirm the first sacral was a dorsosacral.
Phylogenetic analyses have consistently placed Panoplosaurus in a group with Edmontonia, but its exact position relative to other nodosaurids like Animantarx and Texasetes remains debated.
